Teacher card: Shared values and what we remember
Outcome: Explain one shared value connected to remembrance and respect.
Forty minute route: Arrival 4 min; starter 3; model 6; shared task 7; check 2; independent 12; review 3; exit 3. Pause time is flexible.
Preparation: Print the glue-in strips, the evidence and shared cards, the required visual or data sheet and the route card. Exits go in books.

Prepare the books, glue-in strips, route card, word bank, source cards and captioned model. The organiser is one separate A4 page. Keep answers with staff. Use the fictional source profiles; no pupil photographs or personal objects are required.
Access and regulation: Offer a predictable start, private response and agreed pause. No cold calling or forced personal disclosure. Rejoin at one clearly named next step. Keep teen-appropriate examples and the same learning goal across response modes.
This is learning about religion and worldviews, not worship. Nobody is asked to share a personal belief, family detail or loss.
Assessment: Use six short individual answers plus the shared-value explanation. Keep the RAG private and record the access support separately. A reader or exact scribe does not reduce the judgement.
UAS: no approved unit code is supplied. Match evidence to the centre-selected unit and exact criteria. This pack makes no automatic award claim.
Planning: Return lesson using the Autumn 1 Week 7 outcome: Explain one shared value connected to remembrance and respect.
Resources: Book strip; Week 7 Ruth and Dan source cards; word bank; Week 7 model video.
Adaptations: Use third-person fictional examples. Quiet source-matching alternative; no personal belief, family or loss disclosure.
Teaching sequence: Arrival: retrieve festival comparison and remembrance vocabulary. Collect responses before revealing answers.
Starter: retrieve worldviews, values and light. Offer the word bank.
I Do: use the Ruth and Dan source model. Explain how a named detail supports a shared value. Model answer: see Model and answers.
We Do: inspect the action cards, match each action to a value and explain the named source detail.
Hinge: collect each pupil’s letter and reason before revealing the answer: see Hinge and diagnoses.
Independent: each pupil answers the six short prompts from worldviews, beliefs and values, Diwali, Hanukkah, Christmas and comparison. Offer the agreed route.
Review: give one precise teaching move, ask for a // edit, then recheck with the parallel hinge.
Exit: hear one shared value with a source reason and why different worldviews can share it. Pass the private route decision to the next lesson.
LOOP: Check: Ruth prays at a remembrance service; Dan stands in silence. Which value can they share?
Audience: receive each letter and reason privately or through the agreed response mode.
Interpret: use the chosen wrong option’s diagnosis. Silence or an access need is not a misconception.
Teaching move: model the missing action-to-value link. Remove the cue and recheck with the parallel question.
Influence: retain the changed response and adjust the opening example and route for the next lesson.
Target opportunities: Communication and interaction: explain or point to one action-to-value match during We Do. Record the pupil’s own contribution and agreed communication support.
Cognition and learning: choose a source detail at the hinge, revise after a prompt and record later independence.
Social, emotional and mental health: use an agreed help request or pause during Independent, then rejoin at one named question. Follow the individual regulation plan.
Sensory and physical: use agreed pointing, typing, drawing or adapted recording for the book response. Record only a target actually observed.
EAL: pre-teach remembrance and shared value, allow first-language planning and hear the pupil’s own explanation with agreed support.

Capture E against the pupil's own IEDP target on the school's evidence app; the IEDP carries their EHCP-linked and Boxall targets, so one record serves every plan. Follow the pupil's IBSP where it differs from these routines.
If behind: Must-teach core: explain one shared value with a source detail, collect an individual hinge and the six brief check responses. Keep both exit questions.
Can be shortened: extra matching turns, repeated playback and decorative finishing. Use oral or exact scribed answers if recording is the barrier.
Next lesson: choose the opening example and route from the private RAG. Revisit worldview and value vocabulary as needed.
Book evidence and feedback: Record the independent response in the book beneath the dated strip. The six prompts are headings in the book, not spaces on a worksheet. Use the organiser one prompt at a time as a reference.
At Independent, one adult supports access while the other holds the group. Swap this role across the week. Read or scribe the pupil’s exact words without choosing the answer.

VF: verbal feedback when a pupil needs an immediate next step. WS: with support, record the prompt used. I: independent response. NS+: one precise next step in a yellow box. E: evidence against the pupil’s own target in the school’s evidence app. R: record the pupil’s response after Voice, Audience and an NS+ prompt. //: self-edit one detail. ?: read the response back and check its meaning.
At Review, ask the pupil to read back one response (?); name one change, allow a // edit and recheck. At Exit, pass the response and support needed to the next lesson.
Regulate first. Use a short instruction and agreed visual cue. Offer a private response, a pause or space according to the individual plan. Rejoin at one named step when ready.
First lesson back · staff card: Scan a small sample of retained Autumn 1 work for a source detail, a reason and feedback codes. Unclosed next steps from the cover period are history: do not chase them.

Use the Autumn 1 Week 7 model for remembrance and shared values. Teach the key idea, then collect the short individual check in books. Begin from what pupils show today.

Green: names a shared value with a relevant source clue and accurately uses earlier RE examples. Amber: value is accurate but needs a source prompt or one earlier idea revisited. Red: needs direct teaching to connect value with source and earlier vocabulary. A scribe or reader does not lower the RAG; record the access support separately.
Use the private RAG and exact access support to choose the next lesson’s opening example and Supported, Standard or Stretch route. Give one feedback code and one next step. Do not read scores aloud.

Objective: Explain one shared value connected to remembrance and respect. Evidence: six short individual answers and the Week 7 source explanation in books. Evaluate which concepts need re-teaching and how each pupil responded to a quiet route. Autumn 2 belonging begins with worldview, value and respectful comparison vocabulary.

Arrival: select read-aloud or visual word prompts without preselecting answers. Independent: one adult supports access while the other holds the group. Review: give VF, WS, I, NS+, E or R privately and ask for one // edit. Exit: hand the route decision to the next lesson.
Model and answers: Read these pages before teaching. Hide the model during independent assessment.
Question: Name one value that Ruth and Dan share.

Evidence: B A religious response: Fictional profile: Ruth is Christian. At her church service people pray for peace and read out names from the village memorial. C A non-religious response: Fictional profile: Dan is a Humanist. He stands in silence at the town memorial and thinks about how to prevent war.
Think aloud: Respect, gratitude or hope for peace.
Check: Do people have to be religious to take part in remembrance? No. People of all worldviews remember.
Arrival questions and answers: 1. Give one similarity between two festivals of light.
Reveal after responding: Both use light as a symbol, or both bring people together.
Help: Think of people and events.
Reveal after responding: Taking time to remember people and events.
3. Name a value Ruth and Dan can share.
Help: Look at the two fictional source cards.
Reveal after responding: Respect, gratitude or hope for peace.
4. Can a non-religious person take part in remembrance?
Reveal after responding: Yes. People of all worldviews remember.
Starter answers: Write a religious and a non-religious worldview. Christianity and Humanism are examples.
What can a diya symbolise at Diwali? Good overcoming evil, hope or welcome.
Name a Christian belief connected to Christmas. The incarnation: God became human in Jesus.
Shared activity reasoning: Reading out the names on a memorial — Respect — Card B: naming people honours them.
Thinking about how to prevent war — Peace — Card C: Dan reflects on preventing war.
Keeping two minutes of silence — Gratitude and respect — Card A: silence is kept to remember.
Hinge and diagnoses: Ruth prays at a remembrance service; Dan stands in silence. Which value can they share?
A. Only Ruth can show respect because prayer is religious.
B. Only Dan can hope for peace because silence is non-religious.
C. Both can show respect and hope for peace in different ways.
D. They must agree on every belief to share a value.
Reveal: C. Both can show respect and hope for peace in different ways. Ruth prays and Dan stands in silence.
A: Treats religious participation as the only form of respect.
B: Treats a non-religious response as the only hope for peace.
D: Confuses one shared value with identical beliefs.
Parallel hinge after a teaching move: A church group reads names; a Humanist group keeps silence. What can both actions show?
C. That all people remember in the same way.
D. That only a public action shows respect.
Reveal: A. Respect for people remembered. Both actions can show respect without assuming identical beliefs.
B: Shared values do not require identical beliefs.
D: Quiet reflection can also show respect.
Misconception: Only religious people take part in remembrance. Correction: People with religious and non-religious worldviews can remember.
Misconception: Sharing a value means sharing every belief. Correction: People can value respect for different reasons.
Exit guidance: Respect, gratitude or hope for peace, with a detail such as Ruth praying for peace or Dan thinking about preventing war. People can share a value without identical beliefs.
Teaching and evidence record: Model: Autumn 1 Week 7 remembrance and shared values. Individual check: one concept from each of Weeks 1 to 6. Evidence is in the book beneath the strip.
Look for: A shared value explained with a named source detail, accurate earlier examples and a reasoned comparison. Accept accurate equivalents, speech and exact scribing. Check the concept rather than handwriting or length.
Media: Use manual steps for a calm pace. The silent captioned model and transcript are carried from the remembrance lesson. The source profiles are fictional and do not represent every member of a worldview.
Planning and evaluation record: Delivered as planned: Yes / Partly / No
Criteria met by: all / most / some
Any change from the scheme, reason and impact on coverage: ____________________
Exact qualification unit, registration and award criteria: staff to confirm. A completed lesson alone does not award credit.
Sources: Humanists UK explanation of Humanism: https://humanists.uk/humanism/
Source access was checked on 27 September 2026. Offline teaching material remains available.
Planned adaptations: Explicit instruction; scaffolding: Model one source-to-answer link. Read one check item at a time; hide unused cards and fade the sentence stem after a successful response.
Scaffolding; flexible grouping: Pre-teach the key words with the source pictures. Offer silent planning, partner rehearsal, pointing, typing or exact scribing before an individual response.

Cognitive and metacognitive strategies; flexible grouping: Use the predictable nine-stage routine, private feedback and an agreed pause. Keep fictional examples, allow a pass on public speaking, and rejoin at one named step.

Using technology; scaffolding: Offer the normal enlarged print, read-aloud, typing, pointing or adapted grip. Use the manual model controls and reduce motion; assess the RE idea rather than handwriting.
Explicit instruction; scaffolding: Pre-teach the lesson vocabulary with an image and example, allow first-language planning, and distinguish language access from conceptual understanding.
Invite a response · two per route: Name one value Ruth and Dan share.
Respect, gratitude or hope for peace.
Taking time to remember people and events.
How does Dan show hope for peace?
He thinks about how to prevent war at the memorial.
What does a diya symbolise at Diwali?
Hope, welcome or good overcoming evil, in the named tradition.
How can Ruth and Dan share a value without sharing beliefs?
Ruth prays and Dan reflects without prayer; each can value peace for different reasons.
Both use light; Diwali and Hanukkah have different stories and meanings.
